# The Hand That Signed the Paper

"The Hand That Signed the Paper" is a war protest poem by Welsh poet Dylan Thomas . Written in 1933 when Thomas was just 19 years old, the poem was first published in 1936 and appears in Jon Stallworthy's edited collection "The Oxford Book of War Poetry" . The work is a socio-political commentary that critiques the ruthless and indifferent exercise of political power, particularly as manifested in wartime decisions .

## Contents

1. [Text of the Poem](#text-of-the-poem)

2. [Background and Context](#background-and-context)

3. [Themes and Analysis](#themes-and-analysis)

4. [Literary Devices and Structure](#literary-devices-and-structure)

5. [Critical Reception and Legacy](#critical-reception-and-legacy)

6. [Musical Adaptations](#musical-adaptations)

7. [References](#references)

## Text of the Poem

The complete text of the poem is as follows :

```
The hand that signed the paper felled a city;

Five sovereign fingers taxed the breath,

Doubled the globe of dead and halved a country;

These five kings did a king to death.

The mighty hand leads to a sloping shoulder,

The finger joints are cramped with chalk;

A goose's quill has put an end to murder

That put an end to talk.

The hand that signed the treaty bred a fever,

And famine grew, and locusts came;

Great is the hand that holds dominion over

Man by a scribbled name.

The five kings count the dead but do not soften

The crusted wound nor stroke the brow;

A hand rules pity as a hand rules heaven;

Hands have no tears to flow.
```

## Background and Context

Dylan Thomas (1914-1953) was born in Swansea, South Wales, and is widely regarded as one of the most significant Welsh writers of the 20th century . He wrote prolifically throughout his lifetime and is best known for his poetry, though his work has sometimes been described as overly "florid" by critics .

The poem was written in 1933 during a period of rising totalitarianism in Europe, when Germany was beginning to recover from the Treaty of Versailles and Nazism was gaining influence . This context is crucial to understanding the poem's themes of political power and its devastating consequences. The work reflects an era filled with mass death events, including war and disease outbreaks .

Thomas's poem is a war protest piece that specifically derides "the appalling apathy and ruthlessness of the rulers toward ordinary citizens" . It serves as a haunting critique of the indifferent and devastating power wielded by political figures . The poem does not reference specific historical events but rather provides a general commentary on the nature of political power and its consequences .

## Themes and Analysis

### Political Power and Its Consequences

The central theme of "The Hand That Signed the Paper" is the absolute and destructive nature of political power . The poem condemns political power exercised through signatures, illustrating how a single hand's signed paper can topple cities, multiply death, and divide nations .

The opening stanza establishes this theme immediately: "The hand that signed the paper felled a city; / Five sovereign fingers taxed the breath, / Doubled the globe of dead and halved a country" . Here, the "hand" symbolizes political authority, and the act of signing represents the exercise of that authority. The imagery of destruction—cities falling, death doubling, countries being halved—emphasizes the catastrophic consequences of political decisions .

The poem further develops this theme by personifying the hand as a powerful ruler: "Great is the hand that holds dominion over / Man by a scribbled name" . This line highlights the arbitrary nature of power, suggesting that the authority to control others comes from nothing more than a signature on a piece of paper.

### Indifference and Lack of Compassion

Another major theme is the complete lack of empathy or compassion among those in power . The poem repeatedly emphasizes the cold, unfeeling nature of political authority. The final stanza drives this point home: "The five kings count the dead but do not soften / The crusted wound nor stroke the brow; / A hand rules pity as a hand rules heaven; / Hands have no tears to flow" .

This imagery contrasts the powerful with the suffering—the "five kings" (representing the five fingers/political authorities) count the dead but offer no comfort or healing. The phrase "Hands have no tears to flow" emphasizes the emotional barrenness of those in power, their inability to feel sympathy or grief for the human cost of their decisions .

The poem's tone is consistently resentful and melancholy , reflecting the speaker's anger and disgust at the ruling class's indifference to the plight of the masses .

### Transformation of Individual into Tyrant

A subtler but significant theme is the transformation of an ordinary individual into a tyrannical figure through the acquisition of power. The second stanza reveals that this mighty hand belongs to an ordinary person: "The mighty hand leads to a sloping shoulder, / The finger joints are cramped with chalk" .

This imagery suggests that the powerful figure is not a mythical or superhuman being but simply a person whose hand has become stiff from writing (perhaps from signing many documents). The reference to a "goose's quill" (a traditional writing instrument) further emphasizes the human, even mundane, nature of this authority figure .

The poem thus explores how power corrupts, transforming ordinary individuals into instruments of destruction and oppression.

## Literary Devices and Structure

### Form and Rhyme Scheme

"The Hand That Signed the Paper" is structured as a non-lyrical Augustan ballad consisting of four quatrains (four-line stanzas) with an ABAB rhyme scheme . This regular structure provides a sense of order and control that contrasts ironically with the chaotic content of the poem.

The first and third lines of each quatrain follow iambic pentameter with an additional unstressed syllable, creating a feminine rhyme . This rhythmic pattern gives the poem a unique passive quality that complements the theme of apathetic authority.

### Personification

Thomas employs extensive personification throughout the poem to amplify the powers of the hand, treating it as an influential entity acting independently . Lines such as "The hand that signed the paper felled a city," "A hand rules pity," and "Hands have no tears to flow" all personify the hand as a powerful yet callous leader .

This literary device serves multiple purposes: it emphasizes the agency of political authority, creates a more vivid and memorable image, and allows the poet to critique power itself rather than any specific individual.

### Metaphor

The poem makes extensive use of metaphor to emphasize the destructive nature of political power . The most prominent metaphor appears in the first stanza: "These five kings did a king to death," where the five fingers are compared to five powerful kings who have the authority to order the execution of another king .

This metaphor underscores the absolute nature of the power being wielded. The "five kings" represent the complete authority of the hand, suggesting that political power operates with the force of royalty or divine right.

### Imagery

The poem is rich with powerful, evocative imagery that creates a picture of horror and devastation . Examples include:

* "Doubled the globe of dead"—suggesting a worldwide increase in death and destruction

* "And famine grew, and locusts came"—evoking biblical plagues and widespread suffering

* "The crusted wound"—conjuring images of untreated injuries and ongoing pain

These images work together to create a comprehensive picture of the catastrophic consequences of political decisions made without compassion or consideration for human suffering.

### Irony

The poem employs irony to highlight the disconnect between the power of political decisions and their human cost. The phrase "A goose's quill has put an end to murder / That put an end to talk" is particularly ironic. A simple writing instrument (the goose's quill) is credited with ending both murder and peaceful dialogue, suggesting that the tools of bureaucracy and governance can simultaneously create and end violence.

## Critical Reception and Legacy

"The Hand That Signed the Paper" is widely recognized as a significant work in Dylan Thomas's oeuvre and in 20th-century war poetry . The poem is frequently anthologized and appears in major collections such as "The Oxford Book of War Poetry" .

Critics have praised the poem for its powerful imagery and its timeless critique of political power. The work is noted for its "haunting" quality and its ability to capture the devastating impact of political decisions on ordinary people . The poem's themes of power, corruption, and the dehumanizing effects of authority remain relevant across different historical periods .

However, the poem also exemplifies Thomas's characteristic ambiguity, as he offers no specific historical context for the events described . This ambiguity has been both praised and criticized—some readers appreciate the universality it provides, while others find it frustrating that the poem doesn't engage with specific political events or historical moments.

The poem has been analyzed extensively in academic contexts, with scholars examining its use of literary devices, its political commentary, and its place within Thomas's broader body of work . It is often taught in literature courses as an example of political poetry and anti-war literature.

## Musical Adaptations

Several musicians and performers have set "The Hand That Signed the Paper" to music or recorded spoken word versions of the poem . Notable adaptations include:

* Recordings by Carleton Hobbs and V.C. Clinton-Baddeley as part of "Anthology of 20th Century English Poetry, Pt. 2" (1961) 

* A spoken word recording by Richard Burton 

* Various musical settings, including one by composer Gwyneth Walker 

These adaptations demonstrate the poem's enduring appeal and its suitability for performance. The rhythmic quality of the poem, with its regular meter and rhyme scheme, makes it particularly well-suited to musical interpretation.

DYLAN THOMAS

1914–1953

**The hand that signed the paper**

The hand that signed the paper felled a city;

![Image 6: Dylan_Swansea](https://oupblog.wpenginepowered.com/wp-content/uploads/2014/10/Dylan_Swansea-493x744.jpg)

_Statue of Dylan Thomas, Maritime Quarter, Swansea, by Tony in Devon. CC-BY-2.5 via [Wikimedia Commons.](http://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Dylan\_Swansea.jpg)_

Five sovereign fingers taxed the breath,

Doubled the globe of dead and halved a country;

These five kings did a king to death.

The mighty hand leads to a sloping shoulder,

The finger joints are cramped with chalk;

A goose’s quill has put an end to murder

That put an end to talk.

The hand that signed the treaty bred a fever,

And famine grew, and locusts came;

The Hand That Signed the Paper

The Hand That Signed the Paper - meaning Summary
------------------------------------------------

Power Wielded by a Signature

The poem condemns political power exercised through signatures. A single hand's signed paper topples cities, multiplies death, and divides nations. Repeated hand and finger imagery links casual bureaucratic acts to mass suffering—treaties breed fever, famine, and silence. The "five kings" symbolize rulers who tally dead without compassion. Thomas exposes the mechanical, tearless nature of state violence and how written authority hides human consequences.

[Read Complete Analyses](https://www.poetryverse.com/dylan-thomas-poems/hand-that-signed-paper/poem-analysis "Analysis of poem: The Hand That Signed the Paper")
The hand that signed the paper felled a city; Five sovereign fingers taxed the breath, Doubled the globe of dead and halved a country; These five kings did a king to death. The mighty hand leads to a sloping shoulder, The finger joints are cramped with chalk; A goose's quill has put an end to murder That put an end to talk. The hand that signed the treaty bred a fever, And famine grew, and locusts came; Great is the hand that holds dominion over Man by a scribbled name. The five kings count the dead but do not soften The crusted wound nor pat the brow; A hand rules pity as a hand rules heaven; Hands have no tears to flow.

2.description: Dive deep into Dylan Thomas' The Hand That Signed the Paper with extended analysis, commentary, and discussion
2.content:
### Summary

Dylan Thomas's poem "The Hand That Signed the Paper" serves as a haunting critique of the indifferent and devastating power wielded by political figures. Through vivid imagery and stark language, Thomas constructs a universal protest against war and the cold efficiency with which leaders send nations into turmoil. The poem's quatrains expose the far-reaching consequences of political decisions, painting a somber picture of the human cost of conflict.

### The Power of a Signature

The poem begins with a stark portrayal of the destructive impact of a simple signature on a document. This act triggers a cascade of irreversible events, leading to the obliteration of cities and the subjugation of entire populations. The paper's signature symbolizes the grim reality of how easily a line drawn by a pen can dictate life and death for countless individuals. Thomas emphasizes that the instigator of such devastation is not a mythical monster, but an ordinary human being, who, drunk with power, becomes the architect of widespread destruction.

### A Mockery of Authority

Thomas continues to dismantle the illusion of power in the second stanza, mocking the "mighty hand" responsible for such monumental decisions. This hand, he points out, is not extraordinary; it is as ordinary as any other, suffering from ailments like arthritis. The weapon of mass destruction, in this case, is a simple "goose's quill," a mere instrument for signing treaties. This sharp juxtaposition highlights the absurdity of the situation, where significant consequences stem from mundane, everyday actions. The poet's resentment is palpable as he recalls how peace negotiations could have prevented conflict, yet were abandoned in favor of violence.

### The Illusion of Peace

In the third quatrain, Thomas exposes the hollow victory of a peace treaty, which fails to alleviate the suffering caused by war. Instead, the harsh conditions imposed by the treaty breed further misery, with famine and plague descending upon the defeated nation. Through this biblical imagery, the poet underscores the irony and futility of a "peace" that perpetuates suffering and chaos. The power wielded by the "almighty" signature is derided, as it merely amplifies the hardships of the common people.

### The Indifference of Leaders

In the final stanza, Thomas shifts focus to the human cost of war, lamenting the plight of its victims. The "five kings" who orchestrate these conflicts remain detached from the suffering they cause, indifferent to the wounds and deaths they tally. The poet is appalled by their lack of empathy and their self-appointed divine status, as they decide who deserves compassion and who faces destruction. In a poignant closing line, Thomas asserts that hands, which have the power to create such havoc, are incapable of shedding tears for the lives they ruin.

"The Hand That Signed the Paper" is a powerful indictment of the cold, calculating nature of political authority. Through a masterful blend of imagery and irony, Thomas elucidates the tragic disconnect between the leaders and the lives they affect, leaving readers with a sobering reflection on the consequences of such detached governance.

### Style and Technique

Dylan Thomas’s poem "The Hand That Signed the Paper" is a masterful exploration of the power and apathy of authority through the lens of poetic form and technique. This nonlyrical Augustan ballad, consisting of four quatrains, utilizes a unique rhythmical structure and striking imagery to convey themes of governmental indifference and human suffering. The poem’s technical elements, such as its feminine rhymes and accentual syllabic pattern, work in tandem with its symbolic content to evoke a profound sense of disillusionment.

### Structural Complexity

The poem is written in a ballad form, but it deviates from the lyrical tradition with an intriguing use of feminine rhyme. Each stanza follows an alternating rhyme scheme, with the first and third lines composed in a modified iambic pentameter. This meter includes an extra, unstressed syllable at the end, lending a trailing, passive quality to the poem. This stylistic choice underscores the thematic focus on bureaucratic indifference, as the rhythm seems to falter and fade, mirroring the poem’s exploration of official apathy.

### Metrical Patterns and Their Impact

Thomas employs a distinctive syllabic pattern throughout the poem. While the opening stanza features a syllable count of eleven in the first and third lines and eight in the second and fourth, subsequent stanzas follow a pattern where the first and third lines have eleven syllables, the second eight, and the fourth six. This truncated effect in the latter stanzas contributes to a sense of incompleteness, which echoes the poem’s themes. The reader is left with an impression of silence and dissatisfaction, as if expecting more from the metrical structure, much like the unfulfilled promises of political authority.

### Imagery and Symbolism

The poem is rich with symbolic imagery, particularly through the use of synecdoche. Thomas’s depiction of the "hand" that signs papers serves as a representation of ruthless governance, capturing how a simple signature can embody entire systems of power. The "fingers" referred to as "five kings" offer an unsettling, dreamlike quality, suggesting the autonomous and conspiratorial nature of authority. The imagery extends to apocalyptic visions of a devastated world, with "felled" cities and landscapes plagued by destruction, reinforcing the familiar yet haunting themes of bureaucratic detachment and human tragedy.

### Expressive Language and Tone

Thomas’s command of language is evident in the poem's somber but resonant tone. Dynamic verbs in the opening stanza such as "felled," "taxed," "doubled," and "halved" convey a sense of relentless calculation, underscoring the cold mathematics of death. The constant repetition of harsh sounds, particularly the letter _d_ in "doubled," "dead," and "did to death," enhances the poem’s thematic exploration of destruction. Furthermore, Thomas’s disdain for political authority is palpable in his depiction of a "scribbled name," reducing monumental decisions to mere triviality.

### Irony and Pathos

Irony is woven throughout the poem, beginning with the juxtaposition of "paper" and "felled" in the opening line. This imagery presents a cycle of destruction, where the paper, created from a felled tree, becomes a tool for further devastation. The second stanza introduces irony through the depiction of the signer’s fingers cramping with chalk, a medium meant for communication that, paradoxically, hampers expression. The poem’s concluding line, "Hands have no tears to flow," provides a poignant, almost nihilistic commentary on the impersonal nature of power, leaving the reader with a sense of genuine pathos rather than overt outrage.

Through intricate structural choices and evocative imagery, "The Hand That Signed the Paper" illustrates the tension between authority and humanity, rendering a vivid portrait of a world caught in the grip of dispassionate governance. Thomas’s technical prowess and imaginative language merge to create a profound exploration of power’s impact on the human condition, inviting readers to reflect on the frighteningly familiar mechanisms of control that shape our lives.

### The Hand that Signed the Paper: Summary

The speaker says that the hand which signed the treaty destroyed a city, five rulers signed the deal for killing half the population of a country, and those five became responsible for the death of a single king. The speaker then resentfully says that this mighty hand leads up to an ordinary shoulder, teeth belonging to a person (old probably) suffering from arthritis, and who has arthritis Thise aThisthless. The treaty signed by this hand has led to famine, locusts, and deaths. This mighty hand is capable of scribbling the name of the man controlling the faiths of the innocent. The five cruel kings count the deaths and are aware of the destruction they created, but they do not soften. Unlike the hands of go,d which always bless and work for prosperity, these kings’ hands prosper less and lack sympathy. These hands belong to selfish and unempathetic people.

### The Hand that Signed the Paper: Analysis

“The Hand That Singed The Paper” aptly portrays the cruelty and the misuse of power that has been and still is being witnessed by the world. The people with power stand in contrast to the almighty power, the cruel kings’ being the villains in the lives of many rather than being the people’s saviors.

### The Hand that Signed the Paper: Tone

The [tone of the poem](https://beamingnotes.com/2018/05/08/tone-poem-fire-ice/) is resentful and melancholy.

### The Hand that Signed the Paper: Conclusion

This poem is a constant reminder of how the attitude of a person with power can change the lives of many forever and how often history has set an example of people’s lives taking a turn for bad when influenced by those who are powerful.

The Hand that Signed the Paper 

And Death Shall Have No Dominion 

Do Not Go Gentle into that Good Night The Dying of the Light 

Duration 10’10” 

The poetry of Dylan Thomas (1914–1953) is characteristically Welsh and dark. Death is a common topic in his writings. Yet despite the somber imagery, there is often a strength and resilience. The journey of death is described, but not taken. Death is the adversary, not the ruler. 

The Hand that Signed the Paper speaks of the often cruel and deadly power of a signed document—a document of taxation, of treaty or of counting casualties. The five fingers mark the dead, but do not soothe. “Hands have no tears to flow.” And Death Shall Have No Dominion expresses the triumph of the human spirit over death. “Though lovers be lost love shall not.” Do Not Go Gentle into that Good Night represents the fight against death. “Rage, rage against the dying of the light.” The musical expression of these poems places the voice in the low (dark) range. Tempi are slow, and minor keys are prevalent. Only occasionally are major tonalities presented. These passages combine with particularly uplifting phrases such as “Though they sink through the sea, they shall rise again” and “Wild men, who caught and sang the sun in flight…” Near the end of the last song, the poet addresses his deceased father: “And you, my father, there on the sad height...” The voice stays on a constant pitch while the harmony lifts beneath (to the heights), in the Lydian (raised) mode. [One might hear the voice as “perched atop” the rising chords.] This is one of the most personal lines of Dylan Thomas’ poetry. As the poet speaks to his father, the climax of the song comes with the rising phrases of “Rage, rage against the dying of the light.” The final chords are dissonant, marked “with determination and triumph.” 

The Hand that Signed the Paper 

The hand that signed the paper felled a city; Five sovereign fingers taxed the breath, Doubled the globe of dead and halved a country; These five kings did a king to death. The mighty hand leads to a sloping shoulder, The finger joints are cramped with chalk; A goose’s quill has put an end to murder That put an end to talk. The hand that signed the treaty bred a fever, And famine grew, and locusts came; Great is the hand that holds dominion over Man by a scribbled name. The five kings count the dead but do not soften The crusted wound nor stroke the brow; A hand rules pity as a hand rules heaven; Hands have no tears to flow. 

And Death Shall Have No Dominion 

And death shall have no dominion. Dead men naked they shall be one with the man in the wind and the west moon; When their bones are picked clean, and the clean bones gone, They shall have stars at elbow and foot; Though they go mad they shall be sane, Though they sink through the sea they shall rise again; Though lovers be lost love shall not; And death shall have no dominion. And death shall have no dominion. Under the windings of the sea They lying long shall not die windily; Twisting on racks when sinews give way, Strapped to a wheel, yet they shall not break; Faith in their hands shall snap in two, And the unicorn evils run them through; Split all ends up they shan’t crack; And death shall have no dominion. And death shall have no dominion. No more may gulls cry at their ears Or waves break loud on the seashores; Where blew a flower may a flower no more Lift its head to the blows of the rain; Though they be mad and dead as nails; Heads of the characters hammer through daisies; Break in the sun till the sun breaks down, And death shall have no dominion. 

Do Not Go Gentle into that Good Night 

Do not go gentle into that good night, Old age should burn and rave at close of day; Rage, rage against the dying of the light. Though wise men at their end know dark is right, Because their words had forked no lightning they Do not go gentle into that good night. Good men, the last wave by, crying how bright Their frail deeds might have danced in a green bay, Rage, rage against the dying of the light. Wild men who caught and sang the sun in flight, And learn, too late, they grieved it on its way, Do not go gentle into that good night. Grave men, near death, who see with blinding sight Blind eyes could blaze like meteors and be gay, Rage, rage against the dying of the light. And you, my father, there on the sad height, Curse, bless, me now with your fierce tears, I pray. Do not go gentle into that good night. [](https://www.antiwarsongs.org/canzone.php?id=46551\&lang=en) The hand that signed the paper felled a city;

 Five sovereign fingers taxed the breath,

 Doubled the globe of dead and halved a country;

 These five kings did a king to death.

 The mighty hand leads to a sloping shoulder,

 The fingers' joints are cramped with chalk;

 A goose's quill has put an end to murder

 That put an end to talk.

 The hand that signed the treaty bred a fever,

 And famine grew, and locusts came;

 Great is the hand that holds dominion over

 Man by a scribbled name.

 The five kings count the dead but do not soften

 The crusted wound nor stroke the brow;

 A hand rules pity as a hand rules heaven;

 Hands have no tears to flow.

 La mano che firmò il trattato abbatté una città;

 Cinque dita sovrane tassarono il respiro,

 Radoppiarono il globo dei morti e dimezzarono un paese;

 Quei cinque re misero a morte un re.

 La mano possente conduce a una spalla sghimbescia,

 Il calcio rattrappisce le giunture delle dita;

 Una penna d’un’oca ha messo fine all’omicidio

 Che ha messo fine ai negoziati.

 La mano che firmò il trattato produsse una febbre.

 E la penuria crebbe, e le locuste vennero;

 Grande è la mano che ha dominio sull’uomo

 Scarabocchiando un nome.

 I cinque re contano i morti, mala piaga

 Incrostata non curano, la fronte non carezzano;

 Una mano governa la pietà come governa i cieli;

 Dalle mani non scorrono le lacrime.
